3.0.0.en: The Pharisees were a group of Jews who kept up the appearance of piety and held strictly to carrying out the commandments and the traditions of the elders. The meaning of their title is "the separated ones," and they were distinguished by boasting; they were among the fiercest opponents of Christ during His ministry. Among them was Nicodemus, who held a social and religious standing as "a ruler of the Jews," that is, a member of the Supreme Council of the Jews, which included their great men. He went to Christ by night, for two reasons. First: that he might inquire for himself about the person of Christ and not depend on what he had heard.

3.0.1.en: Second: that his affair might not be exposed, so he chose the darkness for this visit; he must have feared that the rest of the Pharisees would learn of this visit.

3.0.2.en: Perhaps we may learn from Nicodemus to go ourselves to the Lord Christ and speak with Him, and to have fellowship with the Holy Bible and the sacraments, instead of being content with hearing about Him only from others.

3.0.3.en: Nicodemus began his speech by showing respect for the person of Christ, calling Him a teacher, a word with a special significance among the Jews, which is not applied to just anyone. He also offered faith, though his faith needed confirmation. And this was the reason for the visit, as we have already indicated.

3.1.0.en: Jesus answered without Nicodemus having asked, and from Christ's answer we understand that the question concerned salvation and the condition for entering the Kingdom. Likewise, in Christ's answering without being asked there is a declaration to Nicodemus that the Lord knew what was within him, and it is also a proof of His divinity.

3.2.0.en: Christ began His answer with an expression He used often: "Verily, verily, I say unto thee (you)," and this expression points to the truthfulness of the speaker, his authority, and the importance of the subject.

3.2.1.en: The sum of Christ's words and His teaching is that salvation is not limited to the Jews (v. 16), but is available to all; its conditions, however, are:

3.2.2.en: (1) Birth from above: this means the birth of sonship to God by the Holy Spirit, which makes us children of heaven, and makes us strangers to evil earthly desires.

3.2.3.en: (2) Birth of water and the Spirit: this is the same heavenly birth as before, but through its visible form in the Holy Sacrament of Baptism. For this reason we see our Church's care in teaching that there is no salvation without the spiritual birth from the waters of holy Baptism, and that the condition of faith alone is not enough.

3.3.0.en: We find a situation that recurs often, and which St. John highlighted: the inability of the human mind to understand the divine purpose. Nicodemus did not understand the meaning of the second birth, and could imagine nothing except entering a second time into the mother's womb. This also happened when the Lord spoke of the destruction of the temple, "His body" (ch. 2:19), and it will occur again in His dialogue with the Samaritan woman (ch. 4:7-14). Yet despite this, God does not leave man without explaining His purpose to him.

3.4.0.en: There is a great difference between one who belongs to heaven by his new birth and one who belongs to the flesh.

3.4.1.en: If we have received the new spiritual nature freely in the sacrament of Baptism, do we walk as spiritual people, or is it the desires and inclinations of the flesh that lead us?

3.4.2.en: Beloved, the Holy Spirit has given you what others cannot understand; do you value this gift and this responsibility? It is a call to think and to ask: in my affairs and my relationships, do I walk as a heavenly person, or am I ruled, like the others, by the law of the world and its materialism?

3.4.3.en: It is also noted that the word "must" gave confirmation and obligation to all Christians of the necessity of being born from above (Baptism).

3.5.0.en: "The wind": the speech here is about the Holy Spirit and His hidden work; you do not see Him materially, but you perceive His action and His effects. If we see a tree shaking with all its leaves and bending, we perceive that it is exposed to the wind and affected by it, without knowing the source of the wind or where it goes ... So it is with the Holy Spirit; we perceive Him by His effects on everyone who has received Him and accepted Him in the anointing of the Myron, or the laying on of the apostolic hands (Acts 19:6). And accordingly, so is everyone who is born of the Spirit: he has received from Him strength, love, wisdom, patience, humility and spiritual insight. Baptism gives us three fundamentals: that we belong to God and not to Satan, that we be stronger than Satan, and that we become inclined to good and not to evil.

3.6.s.en: (2) The importance and loftiness of faith

3.6.0.en: The dialogue continues between Nicodemus' astonishment and Christ's gentle rebuke of him: how is it that you, O teacher and interpreter of the Law, do not grasp the spiritual meanings and the divine purpose? The meaning intended here is that theoretical and literal knowledge is not God's purpose and thought.

3.6.1.en: Such is the state of many of us now: we read the Holy Bible, and we may even teach from it, yet we do not grasp the spiritual dimensions of the word of God, which are grasped only by man's humility before the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and his submission to Him under the guidance of the Church.

3.7.0.en: The Lord Christ adds to His words to Nicodemus, who is still unable to understand, an assurance that His words and His testimony are true. The Lord Christ used the plural of Himself, which is unusual among the Jews, saying: "We ... speak ... know ... testify ... our witness." This is a clear indication of His oneness in the Most Holy Trinity; this Trinity alone is the One who knows, teaches, and bears witness to Himself, and not accepting His testimony and teaching is the ignorance of the material world that rejects God Himself.

3.8.0.en: The direct meaning here is: if you do not accept simple matters, how will you grasp the more difficult truths of the faith?

3.8.1.en: "Earthly things": its meaning here is the earthly spiritual matters necessary for life on earth, such as the second spiritual birth, Baptism. It also means that Christ used an earthly comparison to explain the spiritual meaning, when He connected the earthly wind with the work of the Holy Spirit in the life of the believer.

3.8.2.en: "If I tell you of heavenly things": its meaning is that there is a part that is harder for the mind, yet is at the very heart of the faith, and must be proclaimed and believed, such as His relationship with the Father, "I and My Father are one" (ch. 10:30), and redemption by His death, the resurrection from the dead, the ascension and the sitting at the right hand of the Father, all of which are matters above the level of earthly or material perceptible things.

3.9.0.en: When the Lord Christ's conversation with Nicodemus drew near its end, the Lord began to declare three successive truths about His divinity:

3.9.1.en: The first: that He is God incarnate, who came down from heaven and ascended to heaven and is in heaven at the same time. This means that in the time of Christ's incarnation on earth, He did not leave heaven, in His unlimited divinity, for a single moment; He is in a state of incarnation and ascension continually, as the conjugation of the word "ascended" in the Greek language indicates, for it is not in the past tense as the Arabic language suggests, but in the present perfect tense as in the English language.

3.9.2.en: The second: the necessity of the Son of Man being lifted up on the wood of the Cross for redemption. The Lord Christ referred to what Moses did in lifting up the bronze serpent by God's command (see Num 21:8-9), to rescue everyone who looked at it from the deadly bite of the serpents of the wilderness; this was nothing but a type of Christ hanging on the wood of the Cross, who, by His death, rescued from death everyone who believes in Him.

3.9.3.en: The third: the connection of the free salvation offered on the Cross with faith; Christ by His redemption opened the doors of eternal life to all people, but on the condition of faith in Him.

3.9.4.en: Salvation has become a free gift that does not depend on my worthiness but on the grace of God's love for me. He offered me the Cross and redemption as a rescue, and Baptism as the entrance to it, and gave me life that I might live and enjoy being here with Him, so that I may bear witness to Him and strive for this salvation granted to me, lest I lose it ... Grant me, O Lord, to work out this salvation with fear and trembling (Phil 2:12).

3.10.0.en: These two verses, in their meaning, repeat what preceded them, that faith in Christ is the basic condition for salvation, but they add a beautiful spiritual dimension, which is that the plan of salvation has no cause other than God's indescribable and unlimited love for man ... a love beyond the grasp of the mind ... that the Father should give His only begotten Son to death for the salvation and life of the world. And this incarnation and redemption did not have as its purpose judgment or the satisfaction of divine justice ... how easy it would have been for God to judge His creation with a single word; the harder thing is the giving and the death for the justification of sinners in the blood of Christ ... But whoever rejected this redemption and this love offered by the Father in giving His only begotten Son deserved judgment.

3.10.1.en: Beloved ... what distinguishes the saints from us is their practical realization of this indescribable love, for God's love is above the level of changeable human emotions; it is constant and eternal (Jer 31:3), and likewise it is satisfaction for the soul and the spirit. When the saints realized this kind of love, they left everything for its sake, and they are the ones who gained ... Do we realize this wonderful love as they did? And does our conduct express this love? We do not need to know that God loved us, but to enter with Him into the fellowship of infinite love ...

3.10.2.en: A question we put, beloved, to all of us: what have we left for the sake of the love of Christ, as these did?!

3.11.0.en: This love and this light were not accepted by many, who deserve judgment. St. John gives us the reason for their rejection of this light, which is that they are evil, and everyone who does evil and sin consequently hates the light that exposes these evil deeds and reproves them.

3.11.1.en: The secret of the distance of many these days from God and the Church is that they know where the truth is and where Christ is, but they ignore Him because of their love for sin ... This is contrary to the spiritual man who strives in the divine commandment of love; he has no place except Christ, he draws strength from the Church, and his works bear witness to the work of God in his life.

3.12.0.en: "After these things": a phrase St. John always uses to move the reader from one conversation to another, or from one place to another, or from one time to another.

3.12.1.en: "The land of Judaea": east of the mountains of Jerusalem on the banks of the Jordan, and it is known that the previous conversation with Nicodemus was in Jerusalem.

3.12.2.en: "He baptized": its meaning is that His disciples were baptizing and not He Himself (see ch. 4:2), but what His disciples were doing is attributed to their Teacher. St. John Chrysostom and St. Augustine agree that the baptism of the disciples was not counted as a sacramental baptism like that which the disciples also practiced after the Holy Spirit came upon them, but the former is considered similar to John's baptism in that it was a preparation for repentance only.

3.13.0.en: This verse reveals to us the move of John the Baptist from beyond the Jordan to Aenon near Salim, because of the abundance of water in that new place compared with beyond the Jordan. It is implicitly understood that the increase in the numbers of the repentant drove the Baptist to look for a place where the water was more plentiful than the shallow waters of the Jordan, which confirms that baptism was by immersion and not sprinkling. As for Aenon and Salim, they cannot now be identified geographically, but the commentators agree that they lie west of the Jordan River, near the land of Judaea in which Christ stayed with His disciples.

3.14.0.en: It is understood from this verse that there was a period in which the Baptist ministered during the ministry of the Lord Christ, for the Baptist here had not yet been cast into prison. And we find Nicodemus in (v. 2) testifying to Christ that He performs signs. St. John was careful to mention this, because whoever is content with reading the other three Gospels only believes that Christ's ministry did not begin until after the Baptist's imprisonment, but the truth is that what began after the imprisonment was Christ's ministry in Galilee.

3.15.0.en: The Jews understood the baptisms of John and of Christ's disciples as one form of purification and repentance, and in this they were not mistaken according to their understanding, which was still bound to the Law of the Old Covenant, which contained ordinances of purification ... But the dispute or argument was a comparison between the baptism of Christ's disciples, which was increasing, with the Jews gathering around Christ, and the baptism of John the Baptist and his followers, which was decreasing on the other hand. In this dispute the Jews provoked John's disciples, who in turn went to John, presenting to him what had stirred them, that everyone was going to Christ instead of him, asking John to defend himself and his baptism, which came before the baptism of Christ's disciples.

3.15.1.en: The disciples of John the Baptist forgot his first testimony beyond the Jordan to the Lord Christ, when he said that he was not worthy to loose the strap of His sandal (ch. 1:27), and that He is the Son of God (ch. 1:34). Their emotional attachment, and their following of the Baptist with merely human feelings, made them fall into jealousy at the spread of Christ's preaching. We do the same at times: our love for certain persons and our attachment to them may make us fall into a wrong partiality that keeps us from seeing the truth, and we follow them in everything even if we oppose Christ and His commandment ... Do we not then share the error of the Baptist's disciples?!

3.16.0.en: In these verses the Baptist answers the angry jealousy of his disciples with a kind of calm teaching, clear and frank as well, and the Baptist summarized his teaching in the following points:

3.16.1.en: (1) That he cannot take anything or claim a right that heaven has not given him (v. 27).

3.16.2.en: (2) A reminder to his disciples of what he had said before, that he is the forerunner of Christ to prepare the way and the souls, and that he is not the Christ. (3) How great is the difference between the Bridegroom, the Owner of creation and of the wedding, who has the bride (the souls of the believers), and the friend of the bridegroom, for whom it is enough, as a boast and a glory, that he is a friend who contributed to preparing the bride for the bridegroom without claiming that he has any share in her, and for this reason he considers his joy fulfilled (v. 29), because the Church is the Church of Christ.

3.16.3.en: (4) The Baptist confirms this difference when he declares that the natural order is that "He" (Christ) and His Kingdom must increase because He alone is the Owner of honor, and that he himself must decrease and disappear, so that he may also present all who are with him, his disciples, to Christ the Bridegroom of the true wedding, as if he were saying: when the sun rises, its light [overwhelms] all the lamps. Blessed are you, O Baptist, who were counted worthy to be the greatest prophet born of women. Blessed are you in your humility and the clarity of matters within you, for you did not steal the glory of God for yourself, and you did not take anything that was not given to you. Would that we might learn from you not to think that we are the owners of honor, but merely servants and slaves ... that we attribute all glory and honor to the Lord alone, so that our joy may be fulfilled in Him who saved us, as your joy was fulfilled.

3.17.0.en: The Baptist continues his speech, clarifying the difference between the Lord Christ and any other created being, even the Baptist himself. Every man is earthly, and however great his knowledge and understanding, it is limited because it is earthly, and heaven with all its mysteries has not been unveiled to him. And however much he speaks, he speaks in the language of the earth, which is limited and deficient in understanding heavenly things and expressing them. This is unlike Christ, who alone is "from above," that is, from the Father, and this is the reason He is "above all," because His source is the Father and not heaven only, otherwise any angel whose source is heaven would also be above all.

3.18.0.en: What is meant is that Christ testifies to the truth that He knows and declares. As for the use of the expression "seen and heard," it is the Holy Spirit's use of a human expression to bring the meaning near, for the true testimony that man believes is the testimony of an eyewitness, "by sight and hearing," and it is an allusion to the truth of Christ's testimony even if no man accepts it. And the phrase "and no man receiveth His testimony" is a prophecy of the rejection of Christ's teaching and redemption by the scribes and Pharisees, and the many after them, the Council of the Seventy and the priests.

3.19.0.en: That is, whoever accepted Christ's testimony and believed it has believed and affirmed that God is true, because Christ is God, and because Christ is the Word of God and the One who declares to people the words of His Father, and because He is from God He speaks only the words of His Father ... As for the meaning of "God giveth not the Spirit by measure," it is that the Holy Spirit was given to all the prophets by measure according to what the hearer could bear, and according to the circumstances. But as for Christ, the Holy Spirit is not given by measure, but with the whole fullness of the Spirit, because the measure of Christ's fullness is the measure of God Himself; in other words, because Christ is God, He did not receive a measure of the Holy Spirit, for the Holy Spirit fills Him perfectly just as the Holy Spirit is filled from the wisdom of the Son perfectly, and this is another distinction that the Baptist adds in his testimony about Christ in His difference from the rest of creation, since He is its Creator.

3.20.0.en: "The Father loveth the Son": a new mystery that St. John reveals to us in the relationship of the three hypostases, for love is the language of the Most Holy Trinity ...

3.20.1.en: Likewise this verse shows, indirectly, the divinity of the Lord Christ and proves it, for God says: "My glory will I not give to another" (Isa 42:8). Yet that He should give all the glory to the Son, "hath given all things into His hand," is because the Son is equal to the Father in essence, and all that is the Father's is the Son's, and all that is the Son's is the Father's.

3.21.0.en: St. John concludes this chapter with what he wishes to affirm, and which he spoke of in verses 15, (16, 18): that there is no salvation without faith in the Lord Christ; indeed, this verse is the key and the summary of the Samaritan [woman]
